question: what were comon factors driving revenue growth for all companies
answer:
- No single revenue-growth driver applied to all four companies in FY2024–FY2025. Intel’s total revenue declined in both years: $53.1 billion in FY2024 versus $54.2 billion previously, and $52.9 billion in FY2025. [S19] [S68]

- The clearest shared driver for NVIDIA and AMD was data-center demand:
  - NVIDIA FY2024: generative AI increased Data Center demand. FY2025: accelerated computing and AI demand, particularly for Hopper, drove growth. [S53] [S56]
  - AMD FY2024: higher Instinct GPU and EPYC CPU sales drove Data Center growth. FY2025: strong demand for EPYC processors and Instinct accelerators continued that growth. [S35] [S41]
  - Intel shared part of this trend in FY2025: higher hyperscale server and networking demand increased DCAI revenue, but did not produce company-wide growth. [S71]

- Higher-value product mix and pricing supported a different subset:
  - AMD FY2024: Ryzen demand increased both client shipments and average selling prices. [S35]
  - Intel FY2024: a higher mix of high-core-count server products increased server selling prices despite lower server volume. [S20]
  - Qualcomm FY2025: premium-tier Snapdragon demand supported higher handset chipset prices, favorable mix and higher shipments. [S65] [S67]

- Qualcomm’s growth was more handset- and automotive-led than data-center-led: both businesses grew in FY2024 and FY2025; FY2025 also benefited from higher IoT shipments and vehicle launches using Snapdragon digital cockpit products. [S28] [S31] [S67]

- Bottom line: AI/data-center demand was a shared driver for NVIDIA and AMD, with a narrower Intel segment benefit—not a demonstrated universal driver across all four companies. [S53] [S56] [S35] [S41] [S71]

question: Which revenue growth drivers were shared by NVIDIA, AMD, Intel and Qualcomm in FY2025, and which were company-specific? Check whether each company actually grew.
answer:
- Not all four grew in FY2025:
  - NVIDIA, year ended January 26, 2025: revenue rose 114% to $130.5 billion. [S17]
  - AMD, year ended December 27, 2025: revenue rose 34% to $34.6 billion. [S21]
  - Intel, year ended December 27, 2025: revenue declined $248 million to $52.9 billion. [S25]
  - Qualcomm, year ended September 28, 2025: revenue rose 14% to $44.3 billion. [S30]

- No single revenue-growth driver is established across all four. The supported overlaps were:
  - Data-center demand: NVIDIA benefited from accelerated computing and AI; AMD from EPYC processors and Instinct accelerators; Intel from higher hyperscale server demand. This was not a disclosed Qualcomm growth driver in the retrieved annual explanation. [S19] [S39] [S36] [S30]
  - Gaming: NVIDIA benefited from GeForce RTX 40 Series sales; AMD from Radeon GPU demand and higher semi-custom revenue. [S18] [S38]
  - Automotive: NVIDIA benefited from self-driving-platform sales; Qualcomm from new vehicle launches using Snapdragon digital cockpit products. [S18] [S13]

- Company-specific drivers and qualifications:
  - NVIDIA: Hopper demand for large language models, recommendation engines and generative AI; Ethernet-for-AI networking, including Spectrum-X; and Ada RTX workstation adoption. [S19] [S18]
  - AMD: Ryzen desktop/mobile processor demand and semi-custom game-console SoCs complemented data-center growth. Embedded revenue fell 3%, partially offsetting growth. [S8]
  - Intel: server volume rose 9% on hyperscale demand, but server selling prices fell 4%. Lower client volumes, reduced purchasing incentives, customer inventory reductions and wafer-supply constraints weighed on revenue; data-center gains did not produce consolidated growth. [S36] [S25]
  - Qualcomm: premium-tier Snapdragon handset demand increased pricing/mix and shipments; IoT shipments rose across edge networking, consumer and industrial products. A licensing-dispute settlement added $143 million of revenue. [S13] [S29]

question: Compare the demand headwinds described by AMD and Intel in FY2024 and FY2025. Cite the filings and distinguish annual from quarterly evidence.
answer:
- FY2024 annual evidence — both fiscal years ended December 28, 2024:
  - AMD’s headwinds were concentrated in Embedded and Gaming, not company-wide demand. Embedded revenue fell 33% as customers normalized inventories; Gaming revenue fell 58%, primarily from lower semi-custom revenue. Data Center and Client growth drove overall revenue growth. [S1][S2]
  - Intel described broader pockets of weakness: lower desktop demand; lower server demand in a competitive environment; and inventory reductions by 5G, Altera and Mobileye customers. Notebook volumes improved as customer inventories normalized. [S34][S10][S35]
  - Shared driver: customer inventory correction, but in different businesses—AMD Embedded versus Intel’s 5G, Altera and Mobileye exposures. Intel additionally identified desktop and competitive server-demand weakness. [S2][S10][S34][S35]

- FY2025 annual evidence — both fiscal years ended December 27, 2025:
  - AMD’s original 10-K described mixed Embedded end-market demand, with revenue down 3%. In contrast, demand strengthened for EPYC, Instinct, Ryzen, semi-custom console chips and Radeon products. The annual picture therefore was not a broad demand downturn. [S5]
  - Intel’s client weakness reflected customer inventory reductions and comparison against incremental purchasing incentives offered in first-half 2024. Server demand strengthened among hyperscalers, although competition pressured pricing. Late-year client and server sales were constrained by wafer supply despite demand—not simply by weak demand. [S38][S39]
  - The contrast shifted: AMD retained mixed Embedded demand, while Intel combined client inventory adjustment with stronger underlying demand and supply limitations. [S5][S38][S39]

- Quarterly evidence — distinct from annual conclusions:
  - FY2024: AMD’s Q2 10-Q, ended June 29, reported Embedded inventory normalization and lower Gaming semi-custom revenue. Intel’s Q1 10-Q, ended March 30, reported competitive server-demand weakness and inventory reductions across 5G, Altera and Mobileye. [S41][S42][S49]
  - FY2025: AMD’s Q1 10-Q, ended March 29, still reported lower semi-custom Gaming revenue despite Client growth. Intel’s nine-month 10-Q, ended September 27, reported client inventory reductions but stronger Q3 client demand and hyperscale server demand. These interim observations do not establish full-year weakness. [S47][S53]
